paragraphs.text: # Mathematics or the Verifier? No Detectable Gain from

Mathematics or the Veriﬁer? No Detectable
Gain from Veriﬁer-Filtered Self-Training of a
1.5B Model
Tan Sang Nguyen1 and Duy Anh Tran1
Ton Duc Thang University, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam
52300057@student.tdtu.edu.vn, 52300006@student.tdtu.edu.vn
Abstract. Self-training and reinforcement learning with veriﬁable re-
wards report large gains for small language models, but a rising score
does not show that a model learned mathematics rather than what its
veriﬁer accepts. We study the cheapest form of the loop, generate–verify–
select–train with oﬄine LoRA SFT, on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with the
rule-based veriﬁer math-verify, on held-out MATH-500 and GSM8K ex-
ams (150 problems; 500 in a ﬁnal round) at four learning rates on MATH-
500 and two on GSM8K. No pass@1 or pass@k gain has a problem-level
bootstrap interval excluding zero; in the ﬁnal round, with a corrected
recipe, pass@1 falls 3.2–4.8 points in each of three seeds (mean −4.1).
The design detects only gains of about 10 points of pass@1 (6 in the
ﬁnal round; 80% power, intervals without seed variance, so likely more).
A positive gate fails: training on reference solutions lowers pass@1 by
32.2 points, so the null concerns this recipe and cannot show that self-
training fails. As a post hoc audit we track the share of the loop’s own
correct solutions that a storage defect in our pipeline rejects (about one
in six). It falls by 1.5–2.6 points with intervals reaching zero, matching
a falling \boxed share. Two injected-bias controls, one learnable from
the problem, show no selective avoidance, so the audit has no positive
control and is uninformative about adaptation. Two controls, patching
a rarer defect and removing the ﬁlter, show no consistent diﬀerence but
are dose-confounded or too small to detect one. Scores before the ﬁnal
round use the veriﬁer with the defect.
Keywords: self-training · self-improvement · veriﬁer bias · mathe-
matical reasoning · small language models · veriﬁable rewards · neg-
ative result.
1
Introduction
A common recipe for improving the mathematical reasoning of a small lan-
guage model (SLM) without human annotation is to let the model generate its
own solutions, keep those an automated veriﬁer judges correct, and ﬁne-tune on
them, for several rounds. We call this the Generate–Verify–Train (GVT) loop;
it underlies STaR [20], ReST [13], ReST-EM [12] and rejection-sampling ﬁne-
tuning [18]. But the veriﬁer never reads the reasoning: a rule-based veriﬁer such

2
T. S. Nguyen and D. A. Tran
as math-verify1 only extracts a ﬁnal answer and compares it with the gold, and
it rejects some correct answers written in forms it does not parse (Section 3.2).
The training signal is “was the ﬁnal string accepted”, not “were the steps right”.
The same gap runs through reinforcement learning with veriﬁable rewards
(RLVR), which reports large gains at this scale: GRPO on a single training
example lifts Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B from 36.0% to 73.6% on MATH-500 [15], a
gain whose authors report only 8.6 points beyond format correction, and similar
recipes improve DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B [3] and open base models from
0.5B up [21]. Yet Shao et al. [10] ﬁnd that GRPO with random rewards raises
Qwen2.5-Math-7B by 21.4 points on MATH-500, against 29.1 with ground-truth
rewards. A rising score therefore does not by itself show that a model has learned
to solve more problems, rather than to surface behaviour it already had or to
produce what its reward accepts. In RLVR, per-step false-negative rates on the
policy’s own rollouts have been tracked [4,17], and Egashira et al. report that,
for format-based false negatives, a policy ﬁrst unlearns the behaviour that trig-
gers them. This paper studies the question in the cheapest and most widely
used form of the loop, oﬄine rejection-sampling SFT, where a false reject only
removes a training example, and applies the same kind of per-round false-reject
measurement there, post hoc, for one defect of our pipeline.
We ask: after several GVT rounds, is the model better at mathematics, or
has it only learned to write what the veriﬁer accepts? We ﬁxed four measures
in advance: (i) pass@1; (ii) pass@k; (iii) output style, chieﬂy the share of gen-
erations containing \boxed; and (iv) per-problem transitions (problems added
and lost between rounds). The pre-set reading rule was that “learning the ver-
iﬁer’s style” requires pass@1 to rise, pass@k to stay ﬂat and style to converge
at once. In hindsight the rule is one-sided: it can only ﬁre when accuracy rises
(Section 5.1). The higher learning rates, the controls, the round count and k
at those rates, sample accuracy as primary measure, the termination measures
and the re-scoring for a second veriﬁer defect, and the ﬁnal 500-problem round
(Section 4.6) were all added after seeing earlier runs; all are post hoc.
We detect no improvement at any learning rate, though gains below about 10
points of pass@1 or 3.5–5.5 of sample accuracy could have been missed (intervals
omit training-seed variance, so these bounds are optimistic), and no arm of this
recipe improves, so the result concerns the recipe. The second branch is untested:
the pre-set rule is silent, no run varies the frequent veriﬁer defect, and the post
hoc audit of Section 5.3 is uninformative about whether the model learns to
avoid it. What appears, most clearly at the highest rate, is lower accuracy on
the solutions the model does ﬁnish. A sharp decline in a pooled design does not
reproduce under isolation (Section 4.1), and an isolated design at a learning rate
of 10−5 changed the outputs little (Section 4.2).

Mathematics or the Veriﬁer?
3
– For a 1.5B model, LoRA SFT and one rule-based veriﬁer, no gain is de-
tectable on a held-out exam at any learning rate we tried, with bootstrap
intervals and the smallest eﬀects the design could detect. No arm improves,
not even training on reference solutions, so this is a null for the recipe, not
a statement about self-training.
– A post hoc per-round false-reject audit of one veriﬁer defect, carried over
from RLVR [4,17] to oﬄine SFT self-training. The rejected share falls by
1.5–2.6 points, with intervals reaching zero, matching a falling \boxed share.
The audit is uninformative about adaptation, and two injected-bias controls
showed no selective avoidance (Section 5.3).
– A decomposition of an accuracy decline under a ﬁxed token cap into a
ﬁnished-accuracy part and a cap-share part: at the highest rate, ﬁnished
generations lose 5.5–10.6 points against the untrained model on the same
problem mix, and the cap-hit share rises only at that rate.
2
Related Work
Self-training and its limits. STaR [20] introduced the generate–ﬁlter–retrain
loop, and ReST [13], ReST-EM [12] and RFT [18] formalise it; ReST-EM, which
like us restarts from the base model each iteration, reports diminishing gains
after the ﬁrst round. Yue et al. [19] show that RL raises pass@1 while the base
model wins at large pass@k, and Teacher-Free Self-Training [14] concludes that
self-training “ampliﬁes but does not compound”. Training repeatedly on model-
generated data erodes distribution tails [11], and a narrow selector can accelerate
collapse [9].
RL with veriﬁable rewards at small scale. RLVR with GRPO reports large gains
near our model size: one training example lifts Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B on MATH-
500 from 36.0% to 73.6% [15], about 7,000 examples lift DeepSeek-R1-Distill-
Qwen-1.5B on AMC23 from 63% to 80% [3], and zero-RL works across ten open
base models including Qwen2.5 from 0.5B [21]. These studies improve accuracy,
which our SFT loop does not; of Wang et al.’s 37.6 points only 8.6 lie beyond
format correction. Shao et al. [10] show that it need not be reward learning:
random rewards raise Qwen2.5-Math-7B by 21.4 points on MATH-500, which
they trace to ampliﬁed pre-existing behaviour, and the eﬀect varies by model
family. We do not compete with RLVR on accuracy; the audit of Section 5.3 asks
of a loop whether the model has adapted to one veriﬁer defect, and we apply it
only to SFT.
Veriﬁer error. TinyV [17] ﬁnds that rule-based veriﬁers reject many correct
solutions; From Accuracy to Robustness [6] reports an average recall of 86%,
and 0.95 for math-verify on their MATH subset. Imperfect Veriﬁers [1] models
ﬁxed false-accept and false-reject rates. Egashira et al. [4] ﬁnd in RLVR that
systematic false negatives behave like random noise whereas false positives can
cause plateau or collapse. They also track the false-negative rate on the policy’s

4
T. S. Nguyen and D. A. Tran
rollouts per step and, for format-based false negatives, see the policy ﬁrst unlearn
the behaviour that triggers them. Our setting diﬀers in paradigm (oﬄine SFT
with a fresh adapter per round) and task, and our controls cannot test their
ﬁndings (Section 4.3).
Auditing self-improvement. Xu et al. [16] audit LoRA self-training of Qwen3-
8B against a frozen control and identify seven measurement failures, including
training-seed variance and a ﬁxed token cap under style drift, that each invert
a ﬁnding when uncontrolled. This is the study closest to ours; it is why we
separate ﬁnished accuracy from termination (Section 4.5). We diﬀer in scale (a
1.5B model), in the veriﬁer (a rule-based one whose rejection defect we measured)
and in auditing what that veriﬁer’s ﬁltering does to the training pool, not only
whether accuracy moved. Kim et al. [8] show that self-distillation with a teacher
that sees the correct solution can cut accuracy while shortening responses, as our
train-on-gold control does. Our per-round false-reject measurement (Section 5.3)
is not new: it is the per-step tracking of Egashira et al. and TinyV, applied to
oﬄine SFT and to a defect of our own pipeline, and since our patch control
proved too weak (Section 4.3) we do not claim the combination of a measured
veriﬁer bias and a patched control as a contribution. The PRM800K grader [7]
normalises \dfrac and \frac43 and could serve as a second veriﬁer; we did not
run it. Supplementary Appendix A gives the full comparison.
3
Setup
3.1
The GVT Loop
Each round t has four steps. Generate: the current model samples k solutions per
problem. Verify: math-verify extracts the ﬁnal answer and compares it with the
gold. Select: accepted solutions are kept. Train: a fresh LoRA adapter is attached
to the base model and trained on the kept solutions for one epoch. Round 0 is
the untrained base model; the round-t model (t ≥1) is the base plus an adapter
trained on the pool accepted at round t −1. Adapters are not accumulated, so
earlier rounds aﬀect later ones only through the data they generate; conclusions
about (non-)compounding below apply to this restart-from-base design, which
gives compounding less room than continued training would.
3.2
The Veriﬁer and Its Directional Bias
A format probe that re-renders gold answers in individually valid forms shows
that \dfrac/\tfrac are rejected 100% of the time on both datasets (the com-
mand is not parsed). On real solutions (one public Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct solution
per problem for 200 MATH-500 problems, judged correct by a scripted nor-
malised comparison) the false-negative rate is 7.8% (10 of 128; Wilson interval
4.3–13.8%) on MATH-500 and 0% on GSM8K. Eight of the ten fail when the
whole solution is veriﬁed but pass when only the boxed answer is; most are com-
pound answers, so they are probably largely the gold-storage defect described

Mathematics or the Veriﬁer?
5
below rather than extraction of a wrong token. The audit inspected only rejec-
tions, so it gives no false-positive rate. The veriﬁer also cannot parse 51 of the
500 stored MATH-500 golds (10.2%); these problems always count as unsolved,
and can never enter the training pool. The oﬀset cancels in within-run diﬀerences
only if those problems would not otherwise change, which we did not check, and
not in ratios or levels across partitions (11–18 such problems per exam partition).
The patch. For the control we rewrote \dfrac and \tfrac to \frac before
parsing, removing the 100%-rejection class and nothing else.
The gold-storage defect (post hoc). Our pipeline stores the gold without a de-
limiter, and math-verify applies its full LATEX extraction only inside \boxed{}
or $...$, so a correct boxed prediction can fail against a bare gold (e.g. the
prediction \boxed{\frac{4}{3}} against the stored gold \frac43). Re-scoring
the saved generations with a veriﬁer V ′ that wraps the gold in \boxed{} when
the prediction contains one shows that this defect rejects 15.5–18.3% of the gen-
erations V ′ accepts. It would enlarge the round-0 kept pool by about a ﬁfth to
a quarter (440 →542, +23%), against 0–4 examples for the \dfrac patch, and
it lowers absolute pass@1 by 4.7–8.0 points in self-training. It is bound to the
problem, not to the answer: on the 54–62 problems where it ever ﬁres, it rejects
94–98% of correct answers in every round (87–98% where V parses the gold),
and 29–34 of these problems have a gold the original veriﬁer cannot parse at all,
so no answer form avoids it there. Re-scored, sample accuracy still falls in all
ﬁve runs we re-scored; the original-veriﬁer changes are 0.73–0.85 of the re-scored
ones, an observed ratio that we do not use to rescale other numbers or intervals.
All tables keep the original veriﬁer, the one the loop trained with. Section 5.3
uses this defect for the adaptation audit; Supplementary Appendix B gives the
full analysis.
3.3
Two Experimental Designs
Design P (pooled) loads both datasets (500 problems each) together and trains
one adapter per round on the union of accepted solutions, with selection and
evaluation on the same 1,000 problems. Design I (isolated) uses one dataset and
one adapter per run, and holds out 30% of the 500 problems (150) as an exam
set; generation runs on all 500 problems each round, but only the other 350 can
enter the training pool, and all Design I pass rates are on the exam set. Table S1
summarises them.
Design I has three runs, all Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, ﬁve rounds, k = 8, diﬀer-
ing in one respect each: Run A (MATH-500, original veriﬁer), Run B (MATH-
500, patched veriﬁer) and Run C (GSM8K, original veriﬁer). Runs A and B were
repeated at a second seed; since the seed also sets the train/exam partition, the
repetition draws a diﬀerent 150-problem exam set. Most of the later evidence
comes from higher-rate runs introduced in Section 4.4; Table S4 (Supplementary
Appendix E) lists every run. A “seed” sets the exam partition, the selection set
and the training randomness at once; runs with the same seed share the par-
tition. “Five rounds” means round 0 (the untrained model) and four adapters,
each trained once on the previous round’s pool; “three rounds” means round 0

6
T. S. Nguyen and D. A. Tran
and two adapters, so the round-2 model is a single adapter (about 195 optimizer
steps for Run A at 5×10−4) trained on the round-1 pool. All runs use one model
family, Qwen2.5.
3.4
Models, Data, Training, Metrics
We use Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (Design P uses both,
Design I the 1.5B model only) and the ﬁrst 500 problems of the GSM8K test
split [2] and MATH-500, the 500-problem subset of MATH [5]. The prompt is
a single user turn in the model’s chat template: “Solve the math problem. Put
the ﬁnal answer in \boxed{}.” followed by the problem. Generation samples at
temperature 0.8 with a cap of 512 new tokens; the other decoding settings come
from the checkpoint’s generation conﬁguration (top-p 0.8, top-k 20, repetition
penalty 1.1). Training is LoRA SFT (transformers 5.0.0, peft 0.19.1, TRL
1.10.0 SFTTrainer; rank 16, α = 32, on q_proj and v_proj, LoRA dropout and
weight decay at the library defaults; batch size 2; one epoch; AdamW with linear
learning-rate decay and no warmup; loss over the whole chat sequence, prompt
included; fp16 on one Kaggle T4), with a training sequence limit of 512 tokens
that includes the prompt. Because this limit equals the generation cap but also
holds the prompt, any kept solution longer than about 512 tokens minus the
prompt length is cut in training and loses its ﬁnal answer and end-of-sequence
token (24–26% of the round-0 pool; Section 4.5). All kept solutions are used, so
the number of optimizer steps per round is half the pool size. The learning rate
is 10−5 unless stated otherwise; this value was the default of our training code
and was not tuned (Section 4.4). Metrics per round, on the exam set: pass@1
is the correctness of the ﬁrst of the k samples (one draw per problem, so it
carries sampling noise); pass@k; sample accuracy, the mean over all k samples;
style counts over all generations (boxed, dfrac, dollar, . . . ); and per-problem
added/lost counts between consecutive rounds, where a problem is solved in a
round if at least one of its k samples is accepted. Added minus lost therefore
equals 150 × ∆pass@k, so these counts add only the gross churn behind the net
change, not an independent test. pass@1 was ﬁxed in advance; sample accuracy
was not among the pre-set measures, but it estimates the same quantity from
all k samples with less variance, so after the runs we chose it as the primary
accuracy measure. Claims that rest on it, including the 2.2-point bound, are
therefore post hoc in the choice of measure. “Correct” always means accepted
by the veriﬁer (preset reward), the same veriﬁer that selects the training data.
Uncertainty. For every within-run change (round 0 against the last round) and
every paired comparison of two runs on the same exam partition we report a
95% interval from a paired problem-level bootstrap (10,000 resamples of the
150 exam problems; 2,000 for the matched and audit columns), which respects
the clustering of the k samples within a problem. These intervals do not cover
training-seed variance, which we see only across two or three seeds: the one same-
conﬁguration replicate pair we have ends 3.2 points of sample accuracy apart.
We make no multiplicity correction, so we rest conclusions on patterns across

runs and seeds, not on single intervals. Single proportions use Wilson intervals.
Detectable eﬀects. From the interval half-widths h in Table 2, a change would be
detected with 80% power at the 5% level only if it exceeded about 2.8 h/1.96:
about 10 points of pass@1, 8–10 of pass@k and 3.5–5.5 of sample accuracy on
MATH-500. Because h omits training-seed variance (the replicate pair diﬀers
by 3.2 points and B minus A ﬂips from +5.3 to −7.3 on near-identical pools,
Section 4.4), these are lower bounds: a null here means no gain of at least that
size, probably larger (Supplementary Appendix C).
4
Results
4.1
Design P: An Apparent Collapse
In the pooled design the 1.5B model declines severely and with acceleration
(pass@1 50.0% →18.6%, pass@8 72.6% →48.6%; Table S3, Supplementary
Appendix D), on both datasets (Table S2); the 0.5B decline is small. The ac-
cepted pool contracts every round and \boxed{} falls from 5,608 to 2,693 of
8,000 generations. This design cannot be read causally: one adapter trains on
both datasets’ pools; it scores on the problems it selects from; and it trains on
about 4.5× as many examples per round as the isolated MATH-500 run (3,962
against 872 at round 0). No run separates these explanations (Supplementary
Appendix D).
4.2
Design I at 10−5: Small Declines, a Larger One on GSM8K
On the held-out exam (Fig. S1 and Table S5 in Supplementary Appendix E)
pass@8 ends within 4 points of round 0 in every run. On MATH-500, pass@1
is 2.7–4.0 points lower at round 4, with every interval including zero (Table 2);
sample accuracy falls 1.2–3.2 points, with an interval excluding zero only for
B at seed 0 (A at seed 0 reaches 0.0), and matched ﬁnished accuracy 1.1–4.2,
with intervals that only just exclude zero for A and B at seed 0, which are close
to one replicate. We read this as a possible small decline, not an established
one; what we do not see is a gain of the size the design could detect. Run C
(GSM8K) declines more: pass@1 falls 12.7 points ([−21.3, −4.0]), almost all in
ﬁnished accuracy, but it took about twice Run A’s optimizer steps, so we do not
attribute this to the dataset alone. On MATH-500 two coarse output statistics,
length and cap-hit share, barely change, which is weak evidence that the adapter
did little (Supplementary Appendix E).
4.3
The Patch Control Could Not Detect an Eﬀect
Runs A and B diﬀer only in the \dfrac/\tfrac patch. At round 4, B minus
A is −0.7 [−3.3, +2.0] points of pass@1 at seed 0 and +0.0 [−2.7, +2.7] at
seed 1 (recomputed from the saved generations; Table 2 lists values from the
run logs that diﬀer by one problem, giving −0.7). This null is uninformative:

\dfrac appears in 0.50–0.73% of generations, so the kept pools diﬀer by 3–4
examples (under 0.5% of the 872-example pool), and at 10−5 the adapter changes
the outputs little anyway. Removing one rare format defect had no detectable
eﬀect, which a prevalence count alone predicts; the frequent gold-storage defect
is present in both arms.
4.4
Higher Learning Rates
Because 10−5 changed the MATH-500 outputs little, we reran Run A at 10−4
(three seeds), 2×10−4 (two) and 5×10−4 (two, with Run B), with three rounds
and k = 4 (Table 1). These runs diﬀer from the 10−5 runs in k, rounds, pool
size and the pass@k metric as well as rate, so only 10−4 to 5 × 10−4 isolates
the rate. At 5 × 10−4 every run declines: pass@1 falls 4.0–11.3 points and the
sample-accuracy intervals exclude zero in all four A/B runs, though same-seed A
and B are closer to two replicates than four. The decline may grow with the rate
on one seed: at seed 1 sample accuracy falls 1.5, 3.5 and 8.3 points across the
three rates, at seed 2 an almost ﬂat 3.7, 3.8 and 4.7. The cap-hit share rises only
at 5 × 10−4. The patch has no consistent eﬀect: B minus A in round-2 pass@1
is +5.3 at seed 1 and −7.3 [−14.0, −0.7] at seed 2, a sign ﬂip from pools that
diﬀer by 0–3 examples: trajectory noise. Style does not separate imitation from
drift: boxed share falls with the pool, which both would produce.

Anatomy of the Decline
This subsection is post hoc and descriptive. Sample accuracy mixes whether a
ﬁnished solution is right with whether the model ﬁnishes within the 512-token
cap at all. Re-tokenising the saved text, we call a generation cap-hit at ≥508
tokens. At the rates where the share does not rise, 40–46% of round-2 MATH-500
generations already hit the cap (Table 1), so the cap binds from the start. At
5×10−4, compared with the untrained model on the same problem mix, ﬁnished
generations lose 5.5–10.6 points, with intervals excluding zero in ﬁve of six runs
(the six include two same-seed A/B pairs, which are close to replicates), while
the cap-hit share rises 2–14 points. The matched measure conditions on which
problems ﬁnish after training, so it is descriptive. A three-part decomposition
attributes 12–30% of the decline to the cap share in the three original seed-1
runs (and −2 and 5% in two further runs) and 52–72% at seed 2 (Table S9,
Supplementary Appendix H). At 10−4 and 2 × 10−4 the cap-hit share does not
rise and ﬁnished accuracy carries the whole change. Train-on-gold is diﬀerent:
responses shorten by more than half and ﬁnished accuracy collapses. Retraining
without truncated examples, or re-scoring at a 1,536-token cap, leaves the deﬁcit
in place (Supplementary Appendix H).

5
Discussion
5.1
Answer to the Research Question
Does the model get better at mathematics? Not detectably. No run raises pass@1
or pass@k with an interval excluding zero, at any rate; in the 500-problem ﬁnal

round pass@1 falls 3.2–4.8 points in each of three seeds. The sample-accuracy
ﬁgure of about 2.2 points is the largest upper limit among observed intervals, a
post hoc ﬁgure for a measure chosen after the runs that omits seed variance, not
a power statement; on the pre-set measures the design could detect only about
10 points of pass@1 and 8–10 of pass@k (6 and 5 in the ﬁnal round). Because no
arm improves and the positive gate failed, the null belongs to this recipe, and
the study cannot say whether self-training in general helps.
Does it learn to write what the veriﬁer accepts? The data cannot settle this.
The pre-set pattern requires pass@1 to rise, which never happens detectably (the
largest rise is +0.7 [−6.7, +8.0]), so the rule’s silence is not evidence against
veriﬁer-style learning. No run varies the frequent gold-storage defect, and the
post hoc audit of Section 5.3 is too weak to show or rule out adaptation to it.
What happened to the pooled collapse? It does not reproduce under isolation;
the pooled design also trained on about 4.5× more examples per round, so we
cannot say whether pooling, selection-set scoring or dose produced it.
5.2
Interpretation
One explanation of the Design P curves is a self-reinforcing shrinking pool shaped
by the biased veriﬁer. The data neither support nor rule it out: the patch tests
a rare bias, and the no-ﬁlter control declines without any veriﬁer but with more
dose. The defensible statement is narrow: removing a rare format defect, or the
ﬁlter entirely, made no consistent diﬀerence at this resolution. Neither control
tests the systematic false positives Egashira et al. ﬁnd harmful in RLVR.
5.3
A Proposed Audit for GVT with a Biased Veriﬁer
Our pre-set rule tied “learning the veriﬁer’s style” to rising accuracy, so it could
not speak once accuracy fell. From post hoc analyses we propose four checks for
self-training with a rule-based veriﬁer, as a protocol for future studies, not as
tested methods.
(i) A per-round false-reject audit. Fix a repaired veriﬁer V ′ that corrects a
known defect class of the training veriﬁer V . At each round t, on the loop’s own
generations, compute
rt = #{accepted by V ′ but rejected by V }
#{accepted by V ′}

If the model learns to write what V accepts, rt may fall over rounds, but it
also falls when fewer answers are boxed, so it is not a clean signal on its own.
This is the per-step tracking of RLVR studies [4,17] applied to oﬄine SFT;
overall rt is not enough on its own (Table 5; rt_audit.py in the repository).
For the gold-storage defect it falls in all three self-training runs we re-scored,
by 2.6, 2.6 and 1.5 points, with intervals reaching or just touching zero. But V ′
diﬀers from V only on boxed predictions, so unboxed correct answers enter only
the denominator, and the fall matches the falling \boxed share among correct

6
Limitations
Unequal training doses confound every cross-arm comparison, and the controls
are underpowered: the patch changes 0–4 training examples, and the no-ﬁlter
and train-on-gold controls have two seeds each. Intervals cover only problem draw
and sampling, not training-seed variance; the ﬁnal-round loop has three seeds,
the gate and the bias controls one, and no multiplicity correction is applied. The
learning-rate grid is coarse and changes k, rounds, dose and metric along with the
rate. The power is limited: with 150 exam problems only gains of about 10 points
of pass@1 would be detected (about 6 with the 500 problems of Section 4.6,
k = 2, two rounds). The adaptation audit is weak: 24–28 problems, 2–12 training
examples per round that could teach avoidance, and two positive controls with
no eﬀect. The veriﬁer audit used other models’ solutions and inspected only
rejections; the gold-storage defect was measured afterwards and ran unvaried
through every run before the ﬁnal round, and every headline number is graded
by the biased veriﬁer that also selects the data. Truncation: the 512-token cap
binds from the start and truncates a quarter of the pool in the main runs. Scope:
one model family and size, all instruction-tuned (no base model), one veriﬁer,
a restart-from-base design that leaves compounding little room (no continued
training), and possible test-set contamination. No arm improves on round 0,
and the gate on reference solutions failed even with the corrected recipe, so we
have no positive reference showing that any recipe can help a 1.5B model here.
7
Conclusion
We asked whether generate–verify–select–train iterations make a 1.5B model
better at mathematics or only teach it to write what a rule-based veriﬁer accepts.
On held-out exams the ﬁrst answer is no gain that this design could detect: no run
shows a pass@1 or pass@k gain whose interval excludes zero, though gains below

about 10 and 8–10 points could have been missed (6 in a ﬁnal 500-problem round,
where pass@1 falls 3.2–4.8 points in all three seeds), and the sample-accuracy
ﬁgure of about 2.2 points is a post hoc upper limit, not a power statement,
that omits training-seed variance. No arm improves, and training on reference
solutions lowers pass@1 by about 30 points even with a corrected recipe, so
this is a null for the recipe, and the failed gate means it says little about self-
training. The second question stays open: our pre-set rule could only ﬁre if
accuracy rose. A post hoc per-round false-reject audit, carried over from RLVR,
is uninformative about whether the model learns to avoid one veriﬁer defect: its
fall matches the falling \boxed share, which adaptation would also produce, and
with about 25 aﬀected problems, a handful of training examples per round and
two injected-bias controls that showed no selective avoidance, it has little power.
At the highest rate the model is less accurate on the solutions it ﬁnishes. Patching
a rare veriﬁer defect and removing the ﬁlter made no consistent diﬀerence, but
neither control could detect a small one. The pooled design’s decline does not
reproduce under isolation.
A per-round false-reject audit asks part of the question whether accuracy
rises or falls, but it must be conditioned on answer format and on the problems
where the defect can be avoided, and it needs a positive control. A dose-matched
control for the gold-storage defect and a recipe that passes the positive gate come
ﬁrst (Supplementary Appendix K).

openaireview__claude.label: OpenAIReview (claude)
openaireview__claude.overall_feedback: The paper is unusually candid: it reports a null, discloses post hoc choices and states its own power limits, and the arithmetic I recomputed (Wilson interval, t-intervals, detectable-effect constant, table identities) is largely correct. The central weakness is that the null cannot support its framing. The failed positive gate (reference-solution training collapses by 32 points) points to a pipeline defect, so no result can be attributed to self-training or to the verifier; every score is graded by the defective verifier; and the pre-set measures have little power. The r_t audit is partly an algebraic identity (boxed-only r_t × boxed share), and the injected-bias controls are neither valid positive controls nor consistently reported. Standards are also applied unevenly (no multiplicity correction, small declines read as real). These issues are fixable mostly by reframing and cheap re-scoring with V' on saved generations.

comments.title: Title/'negative result' framing outruns a design that cannot answer either branch
comments.quote: The design detects only gains of about 10 points of pass@1 (6 in the
comments.explanation: The paper's own evidence says the null belongs to a recipe it describes as flawed (loss on the prompt, q/v-only LoRA, 512 cap truncating a quarter of the pool, untuned LR), the gate failed, the design detects only ~10 (6) points of pass@1, and every score is produced by the verifier under study. The title question (mathematics or the verifier?) is therefore answered on neither side, and no matched-dose unfiltered/random baseline or V'-trained run (cheap, since V' exists) manipulates the verifier. The paper is candid about this in places, but title, keywords and the Conclusion's 'no' still read as a finding about verifier-filtered self-training.

comments.title: Failed positive gate invalidates the 'corrected recipe' label and the gate as a control
comments.quote: The gate shows only that we have no recipe known to raise accuracy;
comments.explanation: A 32-point collapse from 300 reference solutions (unchanged at 2e-5) points to a pipeline defect rather than a property of the task, yet the recipe is called 'corrected' in the abstract and §4.6. Seven recipe changes were made at once with no ablation, the $-style attribution is asserted not tested, and a harmful configuration could equally explain the loop's own decline. The gate is therefore not a valid positive control and the −4.1 mean cannot be attributed to self-training or to the verifier.

comments.title: All scores use the training verifier that the paper shows to be defective
comments.quote: through every run before the ﬁnal round, and every headline number is graded
comments.explanation: Every headline accuracy is graded by math-verify with a defect rejecting ~1/6 of correct answers and 10.2% unparseable golds; the defect interacts with training-induced format changes (boxed share, $-style), so it does not cancel in within-run differences. The final round normalises gold, so it is not comparable to earlier rounds yet is pooled with them in the abstract/§5.1. A second grader (PRM800K, or V' on the exam) is cheap on saved generations and would allow the stated question to be addressed.

comments.title: Power analysis: single-draw pass@1 on 150 problems, post hoc bounds that disagree
comments.quote: The design detects only gains of about 10 points of pass@1 (6 in the
comments.explanation: The pre-set pass@1 uses one of k samples and cannot detect plausible gains; sample accuracy has about half the minimum detectable effect but was chosen post hoc. The 2.8h/1.96 constant is correct for a two-sided test, but the 2.2-point figure ('largest upper limit among observed intervals') and the 3.5–5.5 bound are two non-reconciled quantities and neither includes seed variance, so 'no gain of at least that size' is not what 80% power licenses.

comments.title: Inconsistent standards: multiplicity, pattern-reading and forking paths
comments.quote: We read this as a possible small decline, not an established
comments.explanation: §3.4 disclaims multiplicity correction and rests conclusions on 'patterns across runs', yet runs share exam partitions and round-0 draws and are not independent. Small declines are read as 'probably costs a few points' (below the stated 6-pt detectable effect) while gains of similar size are dismissed; sample accuracy is negative in 9/9 runs at ≤2e-4 and pass@1 in 12/13 A/B runs, which a pooled analysis would treat as evidence. The same leniency is applied to the r_t pattern (three same-sign falls, all intervals touching zero). Recipe, metric and runs were chosen after seeing MATH-500 results.

comments.title: Replicate/seed-variance evidence is unidentified and the +5.3/−7.3 'flip' is weak
comments.quote: is +5.3 at seed 1 and −7.3 [−14.0, −0.7] at seed 2, a sign ﬂip from pools that
comments.explanation: The only evidence that intervals understate uncertainty is one unidentified 'replicate pair' (3.2 pts) and a B−A sign flip in single-draw pass@1 whose resampling SD for a difference is ≈5 points. 'Seed' bundles partition, selection set and training randomness, so training-seed variance is never isolated and same-seed A/B are called 'closer to replicates' without a test.

comments.title: Prose and Table 2 disagree on the seed-1 B−A difference at 1e-5
comments.quote: A is −0.7 [−3.3, +2.0] points of pass@1 at seed 0 and +0.0 [−2.7, +2.7] at
comments.explanation: Text gives B−A = +0.0 at seed 1, Table 2 implies −0.7 (the note says some values differ by one problem without saying which seed), which also affects the '2.7–4.0' range.

comments.title: 'Pooled decline does not reproduce under isolation' is contradicted or unsupported
comments.quote: A sharp decline in a pooled design does not
comments.explanation: §4.1/5.1 say the designs cannot be compared, while the Introduction/Conclusion assert non-reproduction. Run C (GSM8K) falls 12.7 pts with an interval excluding zero, and isolated 5e-4 runs decline. Selection==eval can only inflate accuracy so cannot explain a collapse, and '4.5× dose' (examples) ignores steps×LR; pooling and dose are inseparable.

comments.title: Rate dependence not shown; the 1e-5 runs are near-null by construction
comments.quote: length and cap-hit share, barely change, which is weak evidence that the adapter
comments.explanation: Sample-accuracy change is about −2.1 at both 1e-5 and 1e-4 and flat at seed 2, undercutting 'the adapter did little at 1e-5' and 'the decline may grow with rate' (one seed). Main 1e-5 runs use an untuned, near-no-op adapter, so the null there is uninformative about self-training.

comments.title: 'No gain at any learning rate' overstates a non-controlled sweep
comments.quote: – For a 1.5B model, LoRA SFT and one rule-based veriﬁer, no gain is de-
comments.explanation: The 1e-5 and higher-rate runs differ in k, rounds, pool size and pass@k metric, so only 1e-4→5e-4 isolates rate; the grid is four points.

comments.title: Cap-share decomposition is unstable and the 'finished accuracy' contribution is overstated
comments.quote: attributes 12–30% of the decline to the cap share in the three original seed-1
comments.explanation: Shares range −2% to 96% by seed, are conditioned on a post-treatment variable, and a crude Table 1 check gives ~96% (not 52–72%) at seed 2 while matched finished accuracy (−5.5) exceeds the total decline (−4.7). The '5.5–10.6' contribution mixes in the no-filter control (10.6) and a run whose interval includes zero; for A/B alone the range is 5.5–9.1. Token counts behind it were not saved.

comments.title: Cross-arm comparisons rest on unmatched dose; no-filter comparison is selective
comments.quote: it took about twice Run A’s optimizer steps
comments.explanation: Run C (~2× steps), no-filter (3–4×) and pooled (4.5×) are used for causal readings. The no-filter vs filtered comparison is summarised by pass@4 alone; pass@1 (+4.0/−4.6) and sample accuracy (+0.1/−5.5) are inconsistent, and at 3.6× steps the seed-1 no-filter decline is no larger, contradicting the paper's dose reasoning. Pool differences are quoted as 0–4, 3–4 and 0–3 in different sections with mixed units (examples vs problems).

comments.title: r_t 'matches boxed share' is an identity, and the train-on-gold rise is not a boxed-share effect
comments.quote: On boxed answers alone rt is ﬂat (changes
comments.explanation: r_t(all) = r_t(boxed-only) × boxed share holds by construction, so the 'match' is not evidence. Boxed-only intervals contain the whole −2.6 fall (so 'flat' is unsupported); for train-on-gold the share part is ~+0.6–0.7 while the boxed-only part (+2.6, +1.6) is ~75–80% of the rise, i.e., boxed-only r_t drifts with no verifier. The claim that adaptation 'would also produce' a 15-point global boxed fall conflicts with only 3–12 avoidance examples and with the hash control, where boxing falls on affected and unaffected problems alike. The available no-filter arm is a missing negative control.

comments.title: 'Pressure to adapt is weak' and the RLVR contrast are asserted, not tested
comments.quote: pressure to adapt is therefore weak.
comments.explanation: The inference comes from a count of pool examples with no dose–response, and conflicts with 'little power to see any'. Rejection-sampling SFT is a positive-only policy-gradient step, so 'a direct pressure SFT lacks' is untested; the 440→542 dose (a fifth to a quarter) is not reconciled with 2–12 avoidance examples.

comments.title: Injected-bias controls: not positive controls, unclear denominators, wrong-direction results
comments.quote: As positive controls for the audit we reran the loop once each
comments.explanation: The hash control cannot elicit selective avoidance by construction; the \frac control is a single run at the final recipe, reports no r_t and no avoidance-example count. '70 of 500' is an exam-set count while selection uses a 300-problem pool, so '263 vs 298' cannot be reconstructed. The visible-rule arm moves +2.8 vs −3.7/−2.7/−5.5 in unbiased seeds (the wrong direction for avoidance) and pass@1 falls 7.0 with an interval excluding zero, yet the text concludes 'neither control shows an effect'.

comments.title: r_t definition and defect statistics: unvalidated V', conflated denominators, ex post subsets
comments.quote: known defect class of the training veriﬁer V .
comments.explanation: r_t treats V' acceptance as ground truth (no false-positive check), includes outcomes the audit cannot affect in the denominator, and 'affected, parseable' is selected on the run's own outputs near a 92–95% ceiling ('bound to the problem' is circular). The independent 7.8% probe (upper 13.8%) does not reconcile with 15.5–18.3% 'one in six'; 542/440 implies 18.8%; the abstract says 'correct solutions' while r_t is over V'-accepted. The framing that the defect is 'verifier bias' is largely the authors' own storage bug, not intrinsic to rule-based verifiers.

comments.title: Audit contribution is internally inconsistent: listed, non-novel and uninformative
comments.quote: – A post hoc per-round false-reject audit of one veriﬁer defect, carried over
comments.explanation: The contributions list credits an audit that Related Work calls 'not new' (Egashira, TinyV) and the abstract calls uninformative, while §5.3 concludes the pressure to adapt is weak. Items (iii)/(iv) are post hoc lessons, not audit checks, and 'dose' is counted in examples rather than steps×LR.

comments.title: Unscorable golds, mixed populations in Table 5, and numeric slippage
comments.quote: 500 stored MATH-500 golds (10.2%); these problems always count as unsolved,
comments.explanation: 10.2% of golds are unscorable and 'we did not check' cancellation although V' makes it cheap; Table 5 mixes trained-on selection problems with unseen exam problems; pool-count definitions differ across caption, prose and Limitations; recomputed Table 5 differences (−5.6, −0.3, +2.2, −0.8) differ slightly from printed ones, and the 91→76%/93→78% shares appear in no table.

comments.title: Token budget and decoding make the exam partly a termination test
comments.quote: prompt length is cut in training and loses its ﬁnal answer and end-of-sequence
comments.explanation: 512-token cap with 43% cap-hit at round 0, 24–26% of the pool truncated in training (answer and EOS lost) and repetition penalty 1.1 at T=0.8 likely depress the baseline and teach unfinished answers, so declines may reflect recipe artefacts rather than self-training.

comments.title: Underspecified training and no pipeline sanity check; reproducibility gaps
comments.quote: weight decay at the library defaults; batch size 2; one epoch; AdamW with linear
comments.explanation: Effective batch 2 with no clipping/warmup at LR up to 5e-4, library-default dropout/decay, seed handling and per-problem sample handling are unspecified. There is no frozen/zero-effect control despite citing Xu et al. as the standard; the gold collapse at two LRs is consistent with a pipeline defect. Design P logs, token counts and the 1,536-token re-scoring were not saved, yet claims rely on them; the AI disclosure does not say which scripts were independently verified.

comments.title: Contamination of Qwen2.5 on MATH/GSM8K dismissed in three words
comments.quote: and possible test-set contamination
comments.explanation: Known contamination affects headroom for self-training, the meaning of small declines, and the MATH-train pool used in the final round.

comments.title: 'Drift' vs 'imitation' is never operationalised
comments.quote: drift: boxed share falls with the pool, which both would produce.
comments.explanation: The no-filter and gold arms decline without any verifier, so generic SFT damage explains the declines equally well; the paper concedes style does not separate the two.

comments.title: Final-round statistics: baseline ambiguity, t-interval, 'all three seeds'
comments.quote:
Change from
each run’s own untrained round 0 to round 1 in points (round-0 pass@1 is 49.2, 46.8,
48.2 at seeds 1–3, from sampling)
comments.explanation: Table 4's 'Untrained 49.2' is seed 1's draw while seeds 2–3 start at 46.8/48.2; the n=3 t-interval omits shared problem-sampling error; '≈6' is a single-run, seed-variance-free figure; 'two rounds' is stated but only round 0→1 is reported; 'falls in each seed' mixes significant (two of three) and non-significant intervals. I recomputed mean −4.07, [−6.08,−2.06] and [−8.05,−1.02]: they match.

comments.title: Cleanliness of the 300-problem MATH-train pool is undocumented
comments.quote:
a pool of 300 problems from the MATH training split, so that the exam is all 500
MATH-500 problems.
comments.explanation: No dedup/overlap check against MATH-500 and no selection procedure; the base model is likely exposed to MATH-train.

comments.title: Final-round loop lacks a no-filter or equal-dose control
comments.quote:
The loop does not help and probably costs a few points;
we did not isolate the cause.
comments.explanation: Without it the decline cannot be tied to the verifier rather than SFT on self-generated data.

comments.title: 'Cheapest, most widely used' loop and RLVR comparison are not like-for-like
comments.quote: This paper studies the question in the cheapest and most widely
comments.explanation: The implemented loop (loss on prompt, q/v-only LoRA, truncated examples, instruct model) differs from standard RFT/ReST, and the RLVR comparisons use base/Math models; the Kim et al. analogy is asserted.

comments.title: Pre-set reading rule has no operational thresholds and little weight
comments.quote: requires pass@1 to rise, pass@k to stay ﬂat and style to converge
comments.explanation: 'Fixed in advance' measures and the rule carry little weight since nearly every operative choice is post hoc, and §5.1 applies it with a post hoc 'detectably'.

comments.title: Corrected-recipe test is one adapter at one rate, not multi-round GVT
comments.quote: It is 10−4 with k = 2 and two rounds; the loop has three
comments.explanation: Round 0 plus one adapter at 1e-4 does not test several GVT rounds, yet 'any learning rate' blends this with the earlier faulty recipe.

comments.title: §5.2 'defensible statement' partly contradicts its own dose caveats
comments.quote: The defensible statement is narrow: removing a rare format defect, or the
comments.explanation: The data 'neither support nor rule out' the shrinking-pool account, yet a statement about no consistent difference is offered as defensible.
